title: Heuristics Biases and Noise
hook: Debiasing training corrects the directional lean. The inter-analyst spread remains. Bias and noise require different fixes.
counterintuition: A heuristic produces both a consistent directional lean and inter-judge scatter. Anchoring makes most analysts adjust too little from a prior estimate (bias) and makes different analysts adjust by different amounts from the same estimate (noise). Debiasing training reduces the average under-adjustment. It does not narrow the spread of individual adjustments. The two problems require different interventions.
tryThisNow: Pick a recurring estimate anchored to a starting number. Bias: does your team under-adjust on average? Noise: do individuals adjust by different amounts given the same information? Each requires a different fix.
keyTakeaway: Heuristics produce both a directional lean (bias) and inter-judge scatter (noise). Correcting the directional lean through debiasing does not reduce the scatter. Both problems are real and require distinct interventions.

breakdown.fastRead:
A heuristic applied to similar cases on different days does not produce a fixed, uniform distortion. It produces a directional lean and a range of distortions around that lean. Anchoring makes most analysts adjust too little from a prior figure; that is the bias. It also makes different analysts adjust by different amounts from the same prior figure; and that is the noise. The two outputs of the same heuristic require different measurements and different fixes.

Debiasing training addresses the directional lean: analysts who learn about anchor conservatism produce larger adjustments on average. The inter-analyst spread (one adjusting 12 percent and another 31 percent from the same anchor) is not addressed by awareness of the heuristic. Debiasing corrects the average error. Calibration of adjustment amounts corrects the scatter.
breakdown.deepRead:
Bias and noise from heuristics are related but separable. A heuristic produces the directional lean by pushing judgment in a predictable direction on average. The same heuristic produces noise by applying that push in different amounts at different times and in different people.

Anchoring research shows that people using a prior estimate as a starting point consistently under-adjust when revising that estimate, producing a directional lean toward the anchor. That is the bias. Anchoring creates bias when every judge adjusts too little from an anchor. But anchoring creates noise when different judges adjust different amounts from the same anchor, or the same judge adjusts different amounts on different days. The directional problem and the scatter problem are both real. Only one of them goes away when you tell people about anchoring. Debiasing awareness of anchor-and-adjust conservatism reliably reduces average under-adjustment but does not reliably reduce inter-judge spread in the amount of adjustment. The scatter requires a different intervention: not awareness of the heuristic, but calibration of the specific adjustment amount to the specific context.

Debiasing training that succeeds at correcting the average error has not touched the majority of the disagreement.

The availability heuristic follows the same structure. Forecasters with recent experience of a dramatic event give higher probability estimates for similar events: that is bias. The degree of inflation depends on how proximate and vivid each forecaster's specific experience was, producing different availability distortions in different forecasters: that is noise. The affect heuristic both inflates average ratings for emotionally vivid cases and amplifies inter-assessor scatter, because some assessors are more susceptible to vivid details than others. Empirical studies in the Kahneman-Tversky tradition, extended through noise audit work, consistently find that the same heuristic generates both components. Measuring only the average directional error misses the scatter that the heuristic also produces.
breakdown.fullRead:
"Both analysts are anchoring to the prior-period target before adjusting for the new earnings data," Oswald said. "The bias is the under-adjustment; on average, everyone moves too little." Marigold put up the second chart. "The noise is the spread around that average: one analyst adjusts 12 percent from the anchor, another adjusts 31 percent, and that gap has nothing to do with what they know. Same earnings release. Same anchor. Different adjustment. That's not a bias problem. That's a noise problem." The debiasing training the team had run the previous year had narrowed the average under-reaction. The inter-analyst price target spread was unchanged.

Bias and noise from heuristics need separate diagnostics and separate treatments. Debiasing training targets average directional lean. Calibration training targets the spread of individual adjustments from the same starting point. Treating one as if it were the other leaves most of the problem intact.

The calibration exercise charts were laid out on the conference table when Theodora arrived. Box-and-whisker plots, two conditions: affect-rich case narratives on the left, clinical-language presentations of the same factual content on the right. The affect-rich condition showed both a higher median vulnerability score (0.7 points, the bias) and a wider box (the 1.4-point inter-assessor range, the noise). The clinical-language condition showed a lower median and a narrower box. The directional inflation from affect-rich framing was real. So was the amplification of inter-assessor scatter. And clinical framing reduced both simultaneously, not only the directional lean.

Desmond's post-season analysis covered a set of hurricane track forecast disagreements. Forecasters with recent experience of a high-impact storm in the forecasted region gave landfall probability estimates 12 percentage points above historical base rate on average, the availability bias. But the inflation was not uniform: individual deviations from base rate ranged from 5 to 23 percentage points depending on how proximate the forecaster's prior experience had been. The same heuristic, different people, different degrees of distortion. That range was noise, not bias, and it was larger than the bias.

If your team has been through debiasing training and still disagrees on comparable cases, you have probably solved the bias while leaving the noise intact. The training corrected the average lean. It did not calibrate how far each person strays from the same anchor. Two analysts who both know they are anchoring and both try to adjust more still adjust by different amounts; those different amounts are the noise that persists.

If the same skater is scored immediately after a high-scoring predecessor versus after a weak one, what changes? The average score drops by 0.3 points in the following-high-scorer condition: the anchoring bias from sequential score comparison. But individual judge suppression ranges from 0.1 to 0.6 points in the same condition. Some judges anchor more to the prior score; some anchor less. The same directional cue, different magnitudes of adjustment in different judges. Randomizing performance order reduces the average effect. It does not reduce the inter-judge spread in sensitivity to whichever predecessor order remains.

You are reviewing the experimental jury data. High anchor demand condition: average award $280,000. Low anchor demand condition: average award $180,000. The anchor created a $100,000 directional difference: bias. Inside the high-anchor condition, individual pre-deliberation awards ranged from $150,000 to $450,000, a $300,000 spread. The anchor inflated the average and simultaneously expanded the plausible range from which each juror chose their individual number. Removing the numerical anchor from opening statements addresses both: no anchor means no directional inflation and no amplification of individual interpretation range.

The board calibration data was on the projection screen when Lysander walked through the findings. Dossiers with citations for operationally dramatic actions: average board member rating 0.8 points above matched non-dramatic dossiers (affect bias), with a rating range of 3.1 to 4.7 across board members (1.6-point scatter). Matched non-dramatic dossiers: 0.7-point range. The dramatic citation doubled inter-board-member scatter while inflating average ratings. Standardizing dossier format to remove affect-triggering language addresses the average inflation and the scatter, because both traces to the same source: the dramatic content that created a large shared upward lean and a loosened constraint on individual board member interpretation.

Every cognitive heuristic that creates directional bias also creates noise by the same mechanism: context-sensitivity. The heuristic's output varies with the contextual cues available at the time of judgment, and those cues differ across people and occasions. The bias is the average of those context-varying outputs. The noise is the variance. Measuring only the average treats the minority of the problem as if it were the whole.

memorableLines.text: Debiasing corrects the average error. Calibration of adjustment amounts corrects the scatter.
memorableLines.why: Pairs the two interventions with the two problems in the shortest possible form, making the distinction immediately actionable.

memorableLines.text: Debiasing training that succeeds at correcting the average error has not touched the majority of the disagreement.
memorableLines.why: Identifies precisely what a successful debiasing program leaves behind: the scatter, which is typically larger than the directional lean that was corrected.

memorableLines.text: If your team has been through debiasing training and still disagrees on comparable cases, you have probably solved the bias while leaving the noise intact.
memorableLines.why: Translates the theoretical distinction into a recognizable organizational experience, giving readers a concrete diagnostic for whether they are in this situation.

examples.title: 12 and 31

planSpec.domain: equity analyst price target: a research quality team studying how anchoring to prior-period price targets produces both directional bias and inter-analyst scatter
planSpec.audience: a brokerage research quality officer studying why analysts covering the same stock produce different price targets from the same earnings release
planSpec.stakes: investor decisions and market credibility — a spread of 20 to 40 percent across price targets on the same company from the same information undermines investor reliance on research
planSpec.requiredBeat: analysts anchor to prior-period targets before adjusting for new earnings data, producing systematic under-reaction (bias); adjustment amounts vary from 12 to 31 percent across analysts on the same anchor (noise); debiasing training narrows the directional bias but leaves inter-analyst spread intact

examples.scenario: "Both analysts are anchoring to the prior-period target before adjusting for new earnings," Oswald said. "The bias is the under-adjustment; everyone moves too little on average." Marigold put up the second chart. "The noise is the spread around that average. One analyst adjusts 12 percent from the anchor, another adjusts 31 percent, and that gap has nothing to do with what they know. Same earnings release, same anchor, different adjustment. That's not a bias problem. That's a noise problem." The debiasing training run the previous year had narrowed the average under-reaction. The inter-analyst spread was unchanged.
examples.whatToDo: Run debiasing training to address systematic under-adjustment from anchors (bias); separately conduct inter-analyst calibration exercises on specific adjustment amounts for comparable earnings changes (noise) to address the spread that debiasing training leaves intact.
examples.whyItMatters: A 19-percentage-point spread in adjustment amounts from the same anchor (12 to 31 percent) produces price targets that diverge substantially even after directional bias is corrected, undermining investor reliance on research consistency.

examples.title: 0.7 and 1.4

planSpec.domain: refugee vulnerability triage: a resettlement agency studying how the affect heuristic produces both directional bias and inter-assessor scatter in vulnerability scoring
planSpec.audience: a resettlement agency quality director studying why assessors give different vulnerability scores to comparable cases
planSpec.stakes: who receives resettlement support priority — affect-rich narratives consistently produce higher ratings (bias) and higher inter-assessor variation (noise) simultaneously
planSpec.requiredBeat: affect-rich narratives inflate average vulnerability scores by 0.7 points (bias) and expand inter-assessor range from under 1 point to 1.4 points (noise); clinical framing reduces both simultaneously

examples.scenario: The calibration exercise charts were laid out on the conference table when Theodora arrived. Box-and-whisker plots, two conditions: affect-rich case narratives on the left, clinical-language presentations of the same factual content on the right. The affect-rich condition showed both a higher median vulnerability score (0.7 points above the clinical condition, the bias) and a wider box, a 1.4-point inter-assessor range where the clinical condition showed a range under 1 point (the noise). The directional inflation from affect-rich framing was real. So was the amplification of inter-assessor scatter. Clinical framing reduced both simultaneously.
examples.whatToDo: Standardize case narrative format to clinical language that conveys factual information without affect-triggering elements; this reduces both the average directional inflation and the inter-assessor scatter that differential affect sensitivity creates.
examples.whyItMatters: When affect-rich framing doubles inter-assessor scatter while inflating average ratings, vulnerability priority allocation is determined partly by which assessor reviewed the case and partly by how affect-triggering the narrative happened to be rather than by actual vulnerability indicators.

examples.title: 12 Points and 5 to 23

planSpec.domain: hurricane track forecast: a meteorological agency studying how availability heuristic effects produce both directional bias and forecast spread
planSpec.audience: a forecast quality researcher studying inter-forecaster disagreement in seasonal hurricane track prediction
planSpec.stakes: emergency management resource pre-positioning and evacuation planning — forecasts that diverge substantially in predicted landfall location produce conflicting official guidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: forecasters with recent high-impact regional storm experience give estimates 12 points above base rate on average (bias); individual deviation ranges from 5 to 23 points across forecasters based on experience proximity (noise); base-rate training reduces bias; inter-forecaster calibration is needed for noise

examples.scenario: Desmond's post-season analysis covered a set of hurricane track forecast disagreements. Forecasters with recent experience of a high-impact storm in the forecasted region gave landfall probability estimates 12 percentage points above historical base rate on average, the availability bias. Individual deviations from base rate ranged from 5 to 23 percentage points depending on how proximate the forecaster's prior experience had been. The same heuristic, different people, different degrees of distortion. The range across forecasters was larger than the average bias. Debiasing training on base-rate anchoring would reduce the average over-estimation. It would not reduce the spread in how much each forecaster deviates from base rate.
examples.whatToDo: Address bias through base-rate adjustment training for all forecasters; address noise through inter-forecaster calibration exercises on cases with documented differences in prior regional experience to reduce spread in adjustment magnitudes.
examples.whyItMatters: When availability-driven deviations range from 5 to 23 points across forecasters on the same case, emergency management receives a forecast range that exceeds the bias by a factor of nearly two, producing conflicting guidance for resource pre-positioning that debiasing training alone cannot resolve.

planSpec.audience: a military promotion board standards director studying why board members give different performance ratings to the same officer candidate

questions.prompt: An equity analyst's price targets systematically under-react to new earnings data and also vary from colleagues' targets in ways not explained by information differences. Which concept best separates these two problems?
choices: Both are symptoms of poor calibration; the analyst needs a more rigorous adjustment methodology that would simultaneously address both the average under-reaction and the variance across analysts.

The systematic under-reaction is bias produced by anchoring to the prior-period target; the unexplained inter-analyst spread is noise produced by the same heuristic generating different adjustment amounts in different analysts. They are separate problems requiring different interventions.

Both are symptoms of the same anchoring process; since anchoring is the common cause, debiasing training that addresses anchoring will reduce both the directional under-reaction and the spread across analysts.
questions.explanation: Option A treats both as the same calibration problem; but the directional under-reaction and the inter-analyst spread are distinct outputs of the anchoring heuristic, and a methodology that reduces average error does not also constrain individual analyst variation in adjustment amount. Option C assumes that debiasing the shared cause addresses both outputs; but research shows that awareness of anchor conservatism reduces average under-adjustment without narrowing the spread in individual adjustment amounts. Option B correctly separates the two problems: bias in the directional average and noise in the adjustment spread are distinct and require distinct interventions.

questions.prompt: A resettlement agency finds that affect-rich case narratives inflate average vulnerability scores by 0.7 points (bias) and expand inter-assessor range from under 1 point to 1.4 points (noise). What intervention addresses both problems?
choices: Require assessors to review equivalent numbers of affect-rich and clinical-language narratives before any scoring session to equalize their affective exposure across case types.

Train assessors to recognize when they are emotionally influenced by vivid case details and to deliberately reduce their ratings in those cases; affect-recognition training addresses both the directional inflation and the scatter.

Standardize case narrative format to clinical language conveying factual information without affect-triggering elements; this reduces both the average directional inflation and the inter-assessor scatter that differential affect sensitivity creates.
questions.explanation: Option A equalizes affective exposure across sessions but does not address the structural problem that affect-rich framing inflates ratings and amplifies scatter for the cases where it appears; equalization of exposure does not eliminate the effect during those cases. Option B uses affect-recognition training to reduce individual ratings; but recognition training does not equalize the degree to which different assessors respond to vivid content, leaving the inter-assessor scatter from differential sensitivity intact. Option C addresses the source: removing affect-triggering elements from the framing reduces both the shared directional inflation and the scatter that arises from different assessors' different susceptibility to that framing.

questions.prompt: Why does debiasing training that successfully reduces average under-adjustment from an anchor not also reduce inter-judge spread in the amount of adjustment?
choices: Debiasing training changes what assessors do on average by making the directional tendency salient; it does not calibrate the specific amount of adjustment each assessor applies, which varies based on individual sensitivity to the anchor and contextual features that differ across occasions and people.

Debiasing training reduces attention to the anchor by making assessors aware of it as a bias source, which removes the constraint that was keeping individual adjustments within a narrow range; assessors now apply less constrained adjustments, increasing the spread.

Debiasing training is effective only for anchoring bias; the inter-judge spread comes from availability and affect heuristics operating simultaneously, which anchoring-focused debiasing does not address.
questions.explanation: Option B predicts that awareness of anchoring would increase the spread by loosening the anchor's constraint; but research does not find this compensatory effect: post-debiasing spreads do not reliably widen, they remain approximately unchanged. Option C incorrectly attributes the inter-judge spread to different heuristics; the spread in adjustment amounts is itself a product of the same anchoring heuristic, as individual differences in anchor sensitivity produce variable adjustments even from the same anchor. Option A correctly identifies the mechanism: debiasing operates on the average directional tendency by making the heuristic salient, but the individual variation in adjustment amount depends on context-sensitivity that awareness alone does not calibrate.

questions.prompt: A meteorological researcher finds that forecasters with recent regional storm experience give landfall probability estimates 12 percentage points above base rate on average (bias) and vary from 5 to 23 points above base rate individually (noise). What should the researcher recommend?
choices: Require all forecasters to use only base-rate statistics and exclude personal experiential knowledge, which eliminates the availability bias and simultaneously removes the inter-forecaster spread caused by different experiential histories.

Address bias through base-rate adjustment training for all forecasters; address noise separately through inter-forecaster calibration exercises on cases with documented experiential differences to reduce the spread in adjustment magnitudes.

Require forecasters with recent high-impact regional storm experience to recuse from forecasts in matching regions, eliminating the differential availability distortion that is the source of both the bias and the noise.
questions.explanation: Option A excludes experiential knowledge wholesale; but experiential knowledge contributes genuine information to forecasts, not only availability distortion, and excluding it would sacrifice relevant expertise to eliminate a systematic bias that calibration can address more precisely. Option C uses recusal to eliminate the differential availability effect; but recusal removes the most experienced forecasters from the regions where their expertise is most relevant, trading availability noise for expertise loss. Option B correctly separates the interventions: base-rate training targets the shared directional bias; inter-forecaster calibration on experiential-difference cases targets the spread in individual adjustment amounts.

questions.prompt: How does an anchor create noise as well as bias in a judgment context?
choices: By shifting the decision away from a more reliable starting point toward a less reliable one; the unreliable anchor creates both a directional distortion and scatter because different judges assess the anchor's reliability differently.

By reducing the information available to the judge; anchoring constrains what information is considered, and different judges under-use different information as a result, producing both directional loss and scatter.

By providing a starting point that each judge adjusts by a different amount depending on their individual sensitivity to the anchor, the contextual salience of the anchor at the time of judgment, and their current decision state; those individual differences in adjustment amount produce scatter around whatever directional lean the anchor creates.
questions.explanation: Option A identifies that judges might assess the anchor's reliability differently, but the mechanism of noise from anchoring is not disagreement about reliability; it is variation in the adjustment step that follows acceptance of the anchor as a starting point. Option B attributes noise to information restriction, but anchoring noise occurs even when all judges have access to the same full information set; the variation is in the adjustment from the anchor, not in the information considered. Option C correctly identifies the mechanism: individual variation in adjustment amount, driven by anchor sensitivity, contextual salience, and decision state, produces the scatter that coexists with the shared directional lean.

questions.prompt: A figure skating federation finds that following a high-scoring predecessor suppresses average scores by 0.3 points (bias) and that individual judge suppression ranges from 0.1 to 0.6 points (noise). What is the correct intervention?
choices: Randomize performance order to reduce the average suppression effect (bias) and separately conduct inter-judge calibration exercises on scoring sequences to reduce the spread in individual judge sensitivity to predecessor anchors (noise).

Implement a mandatory 0.3-point upward correction for all scores following a high-scoring predecessor, which eliminates the directional bias and limits the spread since judges will no longer adjust differently to the same predecessor.

Replace the absolute scoring system with a relative ranking system comparing each skater to the field rather than assigning absolute scores, eliminating the anchor to prior scores and thereby removing both the bias and the noise.
questions.explanation: Option B applies a fixed mechanical correction to the average bias, but this eliminates the bias only if every judge has exactly the 0.3-point average suppression; the 0.1-to-0.6 range means some judges are over-corrected and some are under-corrected, converting directional bias into corrective noise. Option C removes the absolute scoring system, which would eliminate anchor effects; but it may introduce different biases from comparative ranking and does not address the underlying individual variation in anchor sensitivity that a calibration-based approach would target more precisely. Option A correctly matches separate interventions to the two problems.

questions.prompt: A legal research team finds that high plaintiff anchor demands create a $100,000 directional bias in average jury awards and a $300,000 spread in individual juror pre-deliberation awards. A proposed reform limits plaintiff opening statements to factual damage descriptions without numerical demands. Does this address both problems?
choices: Partially; removing the numerical anchor eliminates the directional inflation but leaves jurors to form individual anchors from other case information, which may produce comparable inter-juror spread from those alternative anchors.

No; jury awards are deliberated rather than individual, and deliberation processes compress individual spread before verdicts regardless of anchor design, so neither the directional bias nor the pre-deliberation spread meaningfully affects final verdicts.

Yes; removing the numerical anchor from opening statements addresses both the directional inflation (eliminating the upward pull on average awards) and the inter-juror spread (reducing the amplification of individual differences in response to the anchor), since both components trace to the presence of an extreme numerical anchor.
questions.explanation: Option A correctly identifies that jurors may use alternative anchors from other case information; but the extreme numerical demand is the primary driver of the large directional bias and the expanded spread documented in this study, and removing it addresses the dominant source even if alternative anchors have some residual effect. Option B incorrectly assumes that deliberation eliminates pre-deliberation individual variation; but pre-deliberation individual anchors shape the initial positions that deliberation works from, and evidence shows that deliberation tends to compress rather than eliminate the influence of those initial positions. Option C correctly identifies that both the bias and the noise trace to the numerical anchor: the directional inflation from the high number and the expanded individual interpretation range both disappear when the anchor is removed.

questions.prompt: A military promotion board finds that dossiers with operationally dramatic citations produce average ratings 0.8 points higher than matched non-dramatic dossiers and that inter-board-member spread doubles in the dramatic condition. What should the standards director recommend?
choices: Standardize dossier formats to present operational achievements in consistent, non-dramatic language, which reduces both the average rating inflation from affect-triggering content and the inter-board-member scatter from differential affect sensitivity.

Train board members to recognize when a dossier triggers a positive affective response and to reduce their rating by a fixed amount in those cases, addressing both the directional inflation and the spread through affect-recognition practice.

Remove citations for operationally dramatic actions from initial board review and present them only after board members submit independent ratings, eliminating the affect heuristic's influence on the scoring while preserving the information for deliberation.
questions.explanation: Option B uses fixed-amount reduction when affect is recognized; but board members differ in how strongly they experience affect from the same dramatic content, and a fixed reduction would over-correct for low-susceptibility members and under-correct for high-susceptibility ones, leaving inter-board-member scatter based on different baseline affect levels. Option C sequences the presentation to eliminate affect from initial scoring, which partially addresses the bias; but it does not reduce the underlying inter-board-member spread in affect susceptibility, which would still influence deliberation when the citations are eventually introduced. Option A addresses the source: standardizing format to remove affect-triggering content reduces both the shared upward lean and the scatter from different individual susceptibility levels.

questions.prompt: Why does the availability heuristic create different magnitudes of distortion in different forecasters rather than a uniform directional bias?
choices: Because the availability heuristic is more powerful in forecasters with less domain expertise; expert forecasters develop immunity to availability effects through experience, while less experienced forecasters are more strongly influenced by recent events.

Because availability is sensitive to each forecaster's own experiential history; forecasters with more proximate, vivid, or numerous relevant prior experiences have higher availability for that event type, creating larger distortions in those forecasters than in colleagues with less proximate experience.

Because forecasters deliberately use personal experience as a corrective to base-rate statistics they believe underestimate rare events; the variable distortion reflects different beliefs about base-rate reliability rather than an unintentional availability effect.
questions.explanation: Option A predicts that expert forecasters are less susceptible to availability effects; but research does not consistently support expertise-based immunity to availability heuristic effects; experienced forecasters can be as susceptible as less experienced ones, particularly when their specific domain experience is itself what is made available. Option C attributes the variable distortion to deliberate Bayesian reasoning rather than to the availability heuristic; but the pattern of distortion, correlated with proximity and vividness of experience rather than with explicit beliefs about base-rate reliability, is more consistent with the availability mechanism. Option B correctly identifies the mechanism: each forecaster's individual experiential history determines how available the event type is for them, producing a different distortion magnitude depending on how close and vivid their relevant prior experiences were.

reviewCards.front: How does a single cognitive heuristic produce both bias and noise?
reviewCards.back: A heuristic produces directional bias by pushing judgment in a predictable average direction: anchoring makes most people adjust too little from a prior figure. The same heuristic produces noise because it applies that push in different amounts at different times and in different people, depending on individual sensitivity to the anchor and contextual salience. The average of those individual pushes is the bias. The variance around that average is the noise.

reviewCards.front: Why does debiasing training reduce bias but not noise?
reviewCards.back: Debiasing training targets the directional lean by making the heuristic's average effect salient, which causes people to correct their average tendency. It does not calibrate the specific amount of correction each person applies or when. The individual variation in how far each person strays from the same anchor depends on personal sensitivity and contextual factors that awareness of the heuristic does not address. The scatter persists because the source of scatter is not removed by the source of bias being named.

reviewCards.front: What are the two separate interventions required when a heuristic produces both bias and noise?
reviewCards.back: Bias requires a debiasing intervention that corrects the average directional tendency: making the heuristic salient, providing base-rate anchors, or removing the cue that triggers the directional lean. Noise requires a calibration intervention that reduces the spread of individual responses: inter-rater calibration exercises on specific case types, standardized framing that removes context-varying triggers, or structured protocols that constrain how much individuals deviate from agreed adjustment amounts.

reviewCards.front: How does the affect heuristic create both bias and noise simultaneously?
reviewCards.back: Affect-rich content inflates average ratings for all assessors who encounter it, producing a shared upward directional lean (bias). It also amplifies inter-assessor scatter because different assessors are differentially susceptible to the affective content, with high-susceptibility assessors responding more strongly and low-susceptibility assessors responding less, producing a wider spread of individual ratings than would occur with affect-neutral framing (noise). Standardizing framing to remove affect-triggering elements reduces both components.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean if a team has been through debiasing training but still disagrees on comparable cases?
reviewCards.back: It means the training corrected the directional bias but left the noise intact. Debiasing addresses average error; it does not calibrate individual variation in how far each person strays from the same anchor or frame. If comparable cases still produce substantially different outcomes across team members after training, the problem is scatter driven by differential heuristic sensitivity, and the intervention required is calibration of individual responses to specific case types, not further debiasing.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: For any recurring judgment process where heuristics are suspected, measure both the directional component (is the average systematically skewed in one direction?) and the scatter component (do individuals vary substantially from each other on the same information?) separately. The bias and noise components require different interventions. If you measure only the average, you will design an intervention for the directional problem while leaving the scatter problem intact and undetected.

ifThenPlans.context: When a team produces both systematically skewed average estimates and high inter-team-member spread on the same cases
ifThenPlans.plan: Address the directional bias first through debiasing training or structural removal of the bias-triggering cue (anchoring figure, affect-rich framing). Then measure whether inter-team-member spread has also narrowed. If it has not, design a calibration intervention targeting the spread specifically: inter-rater calibration exercises on the specific case types or contexts where spread is highest, focused on producing agreement on adjustment amounts rather than on the direction of adjustment.

ifThenPlans.context: When a team completes debiasing training and reports improved average accuracy but continued inter-team-member disagreement
ifThenPlans.plan: Do not repeat the debiasing training. The bias problem has been addressed; the remaining disagreement is noise from individual variation in heuristic sensitivity, not from the shared directional tendency. Design calibration exercises that target the cases where spread is highest, focus on getting team members to a common adjustment practice for specific contexts rather than on correcting a direction, and measure success by reduction in spread rather than by improvement in average accuracy.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick a recurring judgment your team makes that uses a numerical starting point: a prior estimate, a precedent figure, a benchmark. Measure both the directional component (does your team systematically adjust above or below that starting point?) and the scatter component (by how much do individual team members differ in their adjustment from the same starting point?). Write down what intervention you would apply to each component. The two answers should be different.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one recurring judgment domain each week, ask two questions about the most recent set of assessments: First, is there a consistent directional lean in the team's average outputs relative to a benchmark or base rate? Second, do individual team members diverge from each other more than case information differences can explain? Track the two measures separately over several weeks. If bias improves but scatter does not, the debiasing work succeeded and a calibration intervention is the next step.
